prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem critiques punitive law and state authority by imagining laws deliberately designed to be broken, using ironic, surreal images of truancy, jail, judges, and police. It suggests that punishment often disguises coercion as care or love, exposing the absurdity and intimacy of systems that claim moral authority while controlling those who transgress.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: State, Make, And

outputs.L1:
So that the truant boy may go steady with the State;  
so that, in his spine, a memory of wings  
will make his shoulders tense and bend  
like something already flown,  
when the bracelets of another school of love  
are fastened to his wrists—  
make a law that need not wait long  
for someone to come along and break it.

So that, in jail, he will have time to read  
how the king was beheaded, and how the hawk that rode  
the king’s wrist died of a common cold,  
and learn that chivalry persists,  
and that what first felt like an insult to the flesh  
was the blank “o” of love—  
put the fun back into punishment.  
Make a law that loves the one who breaks it.

So that no empty court will make a judge recall  
ice fishing on some overcast bay,  
shivering in the cold beside his father, it ought  
to be an interesting law:  
the kind of thing that no one can obey,  
a law that whispers, “Break me.”  
Let the crows roost and caw.  
A good judge is an example to us all.

So that the patrolman can still whistle  
“The Yellow Rose of Texas” through his teeth,  
and even show some faint gesture of respect  
while he cuffs the suspect—  
not ungently—and says things like, “Okay,  
that’s it.”
outputs.L2:
So the boy who skips school can enter a lasting arrangement with the government;  
so some remembered idea of flight lodged in his backbone  
will tighten his shoulders and make them curve,  
as if he were something that had already taken off,  
when the handcuffs of a different kind of loving instruction  
are locked around his wrists:  
create a rule that will not need to wait very long  
before someone appears to violate it.

So that, once imprisoned, he will have leisure to study  
how the monarch lost his head, and how the hawk once perched  
on that monarch’s arm perished from an ordinary cold;  
so he may discover that old codes of honor still survive,  
and that what at first seemed like an affront to the body  
was really love’s empty circle:  
restore pleasure to the act of penalty.  
Write a statute that cherishes the person who disobeys it.

So that a deserted courtroom will not cause a judge to remember  
fishing through ice on a gray bay,  
trembling in the weather beside his father,  
the rule should be compelling—  
the sort no person could possibly follow,  
a command that murmurs, “Defy me.”  
Let the crows settle in and cry out.  
A worthy judge serves as a model for everyone.

So that the policeman may keep whistling  
“The Yellow Rose of Texas” between his teeth,  
and even offer a small sign of respect  
as he places cuffs on the accused,  
not harshly, saying something like, all right,  
that’s enough.
outputs.L3:
The poem imagines a law that does not simply prohibit wrongdoing, but actively draws people toward transgression. Rather than presenting the law as a clear boundary between obedience and disobedience, the poem treats it as something seductive and transformative. To break the law is not merely to fail morally or socially; it is to enter a process through which the self may be altered. The law becomes less like a fixed rule and more like a trap, a test, or even an invitation.

Punishment, in this vision, is portrayed in a deeply unusual way. It is not only an act of discipline or revenge, but also a strange form of love, education, and initiation. Those who are punished are not simply rejected by society; they are drawn into a ritual that teaches them something, marks them, and perhaps even grants them a new kind of belonging. The poem therefore complicates the usual distinction between cruelty and care. Punishment may wound, but it may also instruct; it may constrain, but it may also transform.

The speaker goes further by suggesting that laws should be interesting, tempting, and even impossible to obey. This idea overturns the conventional purpose of law, which is usually assumed to be clarity, order, and compliance. In the poem, however, a law that is too easy to obey would be lifeless. A truly powerful law would awaken desire, curiosity, and resistance. It would reveal something about human nature precisely because people are unable to remain fully innocent before it.

The figures of judges and officers are also presented in complex human terms. They are not merely symbols of authority or mechanical agents of the state. Instead, their roles are mixed with memory, ritual, and restraint. They seem to carry the weight of past judgments and inherited customs, while also performing their duties with a kind of formal care. Their authority is real, but it is not simple. They are part of a system that disciplines others, yet they too appear bound by its ceremonies and limitations.

In this way, the poem challenges ordinary ideas of justice. It refuses to present justice as a clean opposition between guilt and innocence, punishment and protection, law and freedom. Instead, it blends coercion with care, irony with tenderness, and discipline with desire. The result is a vision of justice that is unsettling because it recognizes how punishment can be intimate as well as violent, and how law can both control and create the people who encounter it.
outputs.L4:
The poem offers a sharp critique of punitive law and state authority by imagining a world in which rules seem to exist mainly so that people can be caught breaking them. Rather than presenting law as a neutral system of justice, the poem treats it as something strange, artificial, and even absurd: laws are made with transgression already in mind, as if disobedience is not an accident but a necessary part of the system. Through ironic and surreal images of truancy, jail, judges, and police, the poem exposes the way institutions depend on the very behavior they condemn. The child who skips school, the prisoner in jail, the judge who passes sentence, and the police who enforce order all become part of a distorted moral theater in which authority repeatedly proves its power by identifying and punishing wrongdoing.

At the same time, the poem suggests that punishment is often presented as a form of care. The systems that discipline people frequently claim to act for their own good: the truant must be corrected, the criminal must be reformed, and the disobedient subject must be brought back into proper order. Yet the poem’s irony reveals the violence hidden inside this language of concern. What is called guidance may actually be control; what is described as protection may be coercion. By linking punishment with images of intimacy, care, or even love, the poem shows how deeply state authority can enter personal life. It does not merely threaten from a distance but claims emotional and moral ownership over those it disciplines.

This creates a disturbing tension. The law presents itself as rational, benevolent, and necessary, but the poem makes it appear irrational and almost dreamlike. Its judges and police are not simply representatives of justice; they become figures in a surreal system that creates guilt in order to justify punishment. In this way, the poem questions whether moral authority truly belongs to the institutions that claim it. If laws are designed to be broken, and if punishment is disguised as love, then justice becomes less a matter of fairness than a mechanism of control. The poem ultimately exposes the absurdity of a society that punishes transgression while depending on it, and it challenges the reader to see how coercive power can hide behind the language of morality, discipline, and care.
outputs.L5:
**State, Make, And**

A strong society begins with a clear **state** of purpose. When people understand where they are, what they need, and what they value, they can choose better paths forward. The state of a community is shaped by its people, its culture, its laws, and its shared goals.

To improve that state, people must **make** decisions that support growth and cooperation. They make plans, make efforts, and make changes when something is not working. Progress does not happen by accident; it requires action, patience, and responsibility.

**And** through unity, small actions can become meaningful results. Individuals and communities can work together, learn from one another, and build a better future. The words “state,” “make,” and “and” may be simple, but together they remind us that understanding our condition, taking action, and cooperating with others are all essential for positive change.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem about a law designed to be broken, where punishment is weirdly affectionate and the imagery includes judges, jail, crows, and a patrolman.
counterfactuals.output:
The law was written on dissolving paper  
and pinned to the courthouse moon.

Everyone read it once,  
then immediately forgot how to behave.

The judges wore velvet antlers,  
their gavels blooming with moss,  
and when they declared us guilty  
the walls sighed like tired mothers.

Outside, a patrolman  
with a lantern full of minnows  
walked the avenues backward,  
whistling citations to the crows.

Break this law, the notice said,  
in letters that kept changing into feathers.  
Break it gently.  
Break it before breakfast.  
Break it with both hands full of rain.

So we did.

We stepped on the forbidden shadows,  
kissed the locked doors,  
taught the jail to sing in its sleep.

The crows arrived as witnesses,  
black commas in the white sky,  
arguing over crumbs of thunder  
and the correct pronunciation of mercy.

Our punishment was tenderness.

They sentenced us to be tucked in  
by enormous bailiffs  
with warm blankets and stern mustaches.

They locked us in a cell  
whose bars were made of licorice  
and fed us soup from silver thimbles,  
saying, You know what you did,  
and kissing our foreheads  
with the solemnity of church bells.

The patrolman wept into his badge.  
The judges removed their antlers  
and bowed to the floor.

At dawn, the jail opened like a flower.

We were free to go,  
but the law followed us home,  
small and panting,  
asking to be broken again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary American prose-poem in the style of James Tate, satirizing the justice system with dark humor, absurd tenderness, and unexpected images like hawks, ice fishing, and handcuffs.
counterfactuals.output:
At the courthouse, the bailiff kept a hawk under his coat, which was against policy but not against the law, because the law had forgotten to imagine such a thing. Every time the judge said “sustained,” the hawk sneezed feathers into the fluorescent light. The defendant, a small man accused of stealing a snowblower in July, wept softly into his handcuffs, which had been polished to a mirror shine so he could see the future in them: a room, a chair, a paper cup of water, the moon wearing a necktie.

The prosecutor rose and said, “Your Honor, society is an ice-fishing shack and the accused has drilled too many holes.” Everyone nodded. We had all been cold. We had all been hungry and staring into a black circle, waiting for something silver to make the whole trip worthwhile. Even the jury, twelve citizens selected for their ability to misunderstand lunch, leaned forward with their little pencils poised like oars.

Outside, a siren practiced its scales. Inside, the public defender whispered to his client, “Whatever happens, don’t smile. They’ll think you’re guilty of weather.” But the man smiled anyway, because the hawk had climbed onto the judge’s shoulder and was picking lint from his robe with terrifying tenderness. The judge looked almost happy, or as happy as a machine can look when someone has taped a carnation to it.

“Order,” he said, though no one had ordered anything except justice, which arrived overcooked and missing a fork. Then he sentenced the snowblower thief to three winters of community service teaching fish to repent.

We filed out into the gray afternoon, each of us acquitted of something we had definitely done. The hawk circled the parking lot once, then twice, then landed on the hood of a police cruiser, where it stood like a tiny medieval kingdom. For a moment the handcuffs in the officer’s belt clicked together in the wind, applauding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that begins with “So that the truant boy may go steady with the State” and explores the idea that a good law secretly loves the person who breaks it.
counterfactuals.output:
So that the truant boy may go steady with the State,  
the bell is rung not only to summon, but to forgive.  
The gate swings open on its iron thought;  
inside, the chalk waits like a small white mercy.

A good law does not dream of cages.  
It keeps, folded in its sleeve, a map of the road home.  
It knows the shortcut through the orchard,  
the torn cuff, the lie told badly, the apple bitten twice.

It loves the hand that pockets the match,  
not because of fire, but because the hand is cold.  
It follows the drunk through rain with a lamp,  
muttering statutes like prayers under its breath.

And when the thief stands trembling in the dock,  
his name mispronounced by every mouth but one,  
a good law listens for the child inside him  
still breaking windows just to hear something answer.

Not all law is good. Some is a wall  
built by the rich to keep the weather out;  
some is a boot learning the shape of a face.  
But the good law is different: it blushes when praised.

It would rather be needless.  
It would rather see the boy arrive on time  
because morning itself had called him tenderly,  
because hunger had ended, because fear had slept.

Until then it waits, severe and secret,  
wearing the mask of consequence.  
It takes the runaway by the shoulders  
and turns him toward his own unfinished life.

O love with a gavel in its hand,  
O mercy dressed as a rule,  
do not deny your hidden heart:  
you chase the breaker because you cannot bear to lose him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a strange, lyrical poem about truancy, courts, cops, fathers, kings, and punishment—make it funny, ominous, and philosophical, with long winding sentences and surreal turns.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Truancy King**

On Tuesday, which had been dragged behind the school bus like a tin can tied to a wedding carriage,  
I decided not to attend the algebra of the state,  
nor the spelling of obedience,  
nor the bell that rings in the throat of every child  
until he grows up and calls it conscience.

So I hid in the museum of puddles,  
where the clouds were being cross-examined by their own reflections,  
and a squirrel in a waistcoat accused me of absence  
with the grave authority of a substitute judge  
who has misplaced the difference between law and weather.

By noon the cops arrived,  
riding bicycles made of blue thunder,  
their badges bright as little suns that had been taught to frown,  
and one of them said, “Son, the empire requires your presence,”  
while the other wrote a ticket to my shadow  
for loitering without a measurable purpose.

I told them I had been studying elsewhere:  
the curriculum of ants,  
the civics of broken glass,  
the history of fathers staring into refrigerators at midnight  
as if the cold light might reveal a softer constitution,  
or at least a sandwich not yet ruined by disappointment.

But the law has tiny ears and enormous shoes,  
and soon I was marched to court  
through a corridor where portraits of dead kings  
whispered into their powdered sleeves,  
delighted, as all kings are,  
to discover that childhood can be summoned  
like a debtor,  
like a ghost,  
like a dog that has eaten the crown.

The courtroom smelled of pencil shavings and thunderclouds.  
The judge wore a robe so black  
it seemed to have been sewn from the backs of crows  
who had failed music class,  
and when he struck the gavel,  
the whole room sneezed:  
Order! Order!  
as if order were a disease  
and we were all trying politely to catch it.

My father sat beside me,  
polishing his silence with both hands,  
that old family heirloom,  
passed down from father to father  
like a pocketknife nobody opens  
because the blade might remember blood.

He said, “Your Honor, the boy is difficult,”  
which was true in the way a locked door is difficult,  
or a moon,  
or a joke told at a funeral by someone who understands funerals  
better than anyone alive.

The prosecutor, a man shaped like a filing cabinet  
who had clearly been born during office hours,  
unfurled the charges:  
Failure to Appear,  
Suspicion of Thinking,  
Possession of an Unlicensed Afternoon,  
and Loitering Near the Infinite  
with Intent to Wonder.

At this the kings on the wall began to mutter,  
for wonder is the oldest treason,  
older than bread,  
older than taxation,  
older than the first father who looked at his son  
and mistook obedience for love.

Then the judge leaned forward,  
his wig sprouting small white roots into the air,  
and asked me why I had abandoned school,  
that cathedral of fluorescent buzzing  
where children are folded into chairs  
and taught to raise their hands  
before touching the world.

I said, “Sir, I was afraid  
that if I learned every answer correctly  
I would become a question no one wanted,”  
and the courtroom grew so still  
you could hear the dust practicing resurrection.

One cop chuckled into his mustache.  
Another cop frowned at his chuckling cop-brother  
as though laughter were contraband.  
My father coughed up a whole winter  
and swallowed it again.

The judge consulted a book as thick as a sleeping ox,  
where all punishments were listed alphabetically:  
Apology, Banishment, Chores, Detention, Exile,  
Moral Improvement, Public Example,  
Wearing a Hat That Says I Have Been Corrected.

“Punishment,” he declared,  
“is the broom with which society sweeps crumbs of chaos  
back under the rug of the official breakfast.”

The kings applauded in their frames,  
their rings flashing like tiny prisons for fingers.

But just then the bailiff, who had been a turnip in a previous life  
and still held certain underground sympathies,  
announced that the moon had filed an amicus brief  
on behalf of all absent children,  
arguing that every orbit is technically truancy  
from the straight line.

The courtroom gasped.  
The ceiling opened one bureaucratic inch.  
A flock of report cards flew out  
and migrated south for the winter.

My father looked at me then, really looked,  
not as a broken rule,  
not as a smaller version of his unslept dreams,  
but as a person wearing the weather of his own name,  
and he laughed—  
not loudly,  
not freely,  
but like a rusty gate remembering it was once a tree.

The judge sentenced me to three Saturdays  
of contemplating consequence  
in a room with no clocks,  
one mop,  
and a portrait of a king being bitten by a goat.

The cops escorted me out,  
kinder now, or merely tired,  
their thunder-bicycles ticking in the rain,  
and one slipped me a donut  
shaped like a halo that had lost its argument with grease.

I returned to school the following Monday  
with mud on my shoes  
and eternity in my pockets,  
where the teachers confiscated the mud  
but did not find the eternity,  
because eternity, like truancy, like fathers, like kings, like punishment,  
knows how to sit very still  
when authority enters the room.

And though I learned the multiplication tables,  
and though I stood for the anthem of the pencil sharpener,  
and though I nodded solemnly when told  
that life is mostly showing up,  
I kept, behind my teeth,  
a small illegal bell  
that rang and rang whenever the world grew too orderly,

and its sound was funny,  
because it sounded like a chicken wearing armor,

and ominous,  
because it sounded like a door being locked from the outside,

and philosophical,  
because it would not say  
whether the prisoner was the child who ran away,  
or the kingdom that had to chase him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ironic free verse piece titled “Put the Fun Back Into Punishment,” blending legal language, childhood memory, medieval imagery, and a sympathetic arrest scene.
counterfactuals.output:
# Put the Fun Back Into Punishment

Whereas the undersigned,  
being seven years old  
and sticky with grape jelly,  
did knowingly trespass  
beyond the chain-link jurisdiction  
of Mrs. Alvarez’s yard,

and whereas the apple tree there  
rose like a minor cathedral,  
green-roofed, full of saints  
with red cheeks,

I submit this memory  
into evidence.

The afternoon had no attorney.  
The sun sat high on its bench,  
gaveling everything gold.  
We climbed in sneakers,  
little squires of appetite,  
declaring feudal rights  
over fruit we had not planted.

There were no dragons,  
only a dog named Hector,  
who barked with the grief  
of a village bell.

Still, the law arrived.

Not in armor,  
not on a destrier,  
not with a mace swinging  
at the soft heads of children,

but in the form  
of Officer Daniel Ruiz,  
who knew my mother  
from the pharmacy,  
who carried a radio  
that crackled like burning parchment.

He found me halfway down,  
one knee scraped,  
one apple bitten,  
my face trying to plead  
not guilty by reason  
of summer.

“Come on,” he said,  
as if arrest were just another word  
for helping someone out of a tree.

His hand was large,  
warm,  
official.  
I took it.

The cuffs stayed  
on his belt,  
two small silver halos  
reserved for darker miracles.

Mrs. Alvarez stood below  
in her housecoat,  
a queen among marigolds,  
and sighed the way queens sigh  
when the kingdom is mostly children  
and they are all hungry.

Pursuant to no statute  
except mercy,  
she gave us paper towels,  
salt,  
a knife.

We sat on her porch  
and ate the apple in slices,  
its stolen sweetness  
entered into a plea agreement.

Restitution was ordered:  
one Saturday  
raking leaves,  
two apologies,  
three “yes ma’ams,”  
and a promise  
under penalty of perjury  
to ask next time.

O medieval mercy,  
o municipal grace,  
o bright ridiculous scaffold  
of consequence—

how gently the world once seized me.

How strangely it punished:  
not with stocks,  
not with dungeon,  
not with the village watching  
as shame wore its iron mask,

but with a ride home  
in the back of a patrol car  
whose vinyl seat stuck  
to my knees,

while Officer Ruiz  
turned the radio low  
and told me  
his brother once stole peaches  
from a priest.

Even the law laughed then,  
quietly,  
into its sleeve.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
